paras: The lynching of Willis Alexander was the killing of a 17-year-old Black youth near Baton Rouge, in East Baton Rouge Parish, Louisiana, on the night of August 21, 1890. He had been accused of attempting to assault an eleven-year-old white girl, and his body was found the next day hanging from a tree beside a road. The news reached papers across the country as a short wire item and a one-line digest entry.

According to a Baton Rouge special to the New Orleans Picayune, relayed from New Orleans on August 22, Alexander, described as "colored" and seventeen years old, was lynched "in that parish, last night." The accusation against him was that he had attempted to assault an eleven-year-old white girl; a Baton Rouge brief used the word "rape," and another version said he had tried to "feloniously assault" her. His body was found on August 22 "hanging from a tree by the roadside."
None of the reports names or describes the people who killed him, says how many there were, or explains how he came into their hands. The girl and her family are not named either.
No report of an inquest, arrests or official action appears in the coverage, which ends with the digest items of late August.

Every surviving account comes from the white press and goes back to a single Baton Rouge report. On August 23 the Indianapolis Journal headed it "Colored Boy Lynched," the Richmond Dispatch "Lynched for Felonious Assault," and the Wheeling Register "Lynched a Rapist," a headline that treated the accusation as established. None of these papers added comment, and the Clarksville Daily Tobacco Leaf-Chronicle placed a one-sentence version among unrelated news briefs on August 25.

Weekly papers in Minnesota, Wisconsin and North Dakota then carried a syndicated digest line saying that "William Alexander" had been lynched near Baton Rouge "on the 22d for attempted assault." One form of the digest called him "colored" and the other "a 17-year-old mulatto." No coverage in the Black press was found.

The dated dispatches give his name as Willis and place the lynching on the night of August 21, while the later digests call him William and give the date as August 22. The dispatches stand closer to the original report, and the digest date appears to be the date of the dispatch rather than of the killing.

reader.title: Lynching of Willis Alexander
bases: Every report says Willis (or William) Alexander was 'lynched' and the fullest version says his body was found hanging from a roadside tree (A1, A2, A3).

Alexander was killed by hanging outside any legal process after being accused of attempting to assault a white girl (A1, A2, A3), but no report describes the killers or how many there were, so the group element rests only on the word 'lynching' (A1, A4).

Several papers carried the story (A1-A6), but all of it traces to one Baton Rouge report, which A1 and A2 credit to the New Orleans Picayune's special; no independent local, Black-press or follow-up account was found.

accounts.label: Picayune Baton Rouge special (wire)
accounts.gist: Willis Alexander, colored, 17, was lynched in the parish on the night of August 21 on an accusation of attempted assault on an eleven-year-old white girl; his body was found the next day hanging from a tree by the roadside.

accounts.label: Baton Rouge brief
accounts.gist: Alexander was lynched 'near here last night', accused of attempting to rape an 11-year-old white girl.

accounts.label: Weekly news digest
accounts.gist: 'William Alexander', 17, 'colored' or 'mulatto', was lynched near Baton Rouge on the 22d for attempted assault on an 11-year-old white girl.

framing.detail: The Indianapolis Journal ran the Picayune special under 'Colored Boy Lynched', attributing the lynching and the accusation without comment.
The Wheeling Register's headline 'Lynched a Rapist' and the Richmond Dispatch's 'Lynched for Felonious Assault' turned the accusation into the offense and the stated reason for the killing.
Weekly digests reduced it to one line saying he was lynched 'for attempted assault', placed among accidents, fires and nominations.

conflicts.note: The dated dispatches (A1, A3) are closer to the source; the digest form looks like a rewrite error. A2 prints 'Wilhis', an OCR or typesetting variant of Willis.
